claims.text: High-entropy alloys synthesized as random solid solutions exhibit intrinsic chemical disorder and lattice distortions.
Cluster expansion combined with canonical Monte Carlo simulations can quantify chemical short-range order in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Explicitly incorporating chemical short-range order and lattice distortion will identify low-phonon-conductivity HEAs more accurately than models based only on averaged composition.
The proposed combination of cluster expansion, Monte Carlo, and molecular dynamics captures both local chemical fluctuations and dual-porosity effects.
The relevant thermal-conductivity regime spans approximately 300–700 K.
Controlled annealing can stabilize the desired disordered HEA microstructure.
Chemical short-range order and a dual-porosity microstructure together induce severe lattice distortions.
Severe lattice distortions reduce phonon mean free paths and increase phonon scattering.
Lattice distortion in high-entropy alloys can reduce phonon velocity, enhance phonon scattering, and thereby lower lattice thermal conductivity.
Local chemical fluctuations are directly related to lattice thermal conductivity in high-entropy thermoelectric materials.
Modeling chemical ordering and local structural variation captures the critical physics controlling phonon transport.
Candidates selected by the proposed model will exhibit at least a 15–20% improvement in prediction accuracy relative to conventional methods.
Conventional composition-average models underestimate the effects of local chemical fluctuations and porous microstructures on phonon scattering.
The approach is applicable only when HEAs possess substantial chemical disorder and associated lattice distortion.
The approach may not apply to ordered alloys or alloys with negligible local chemical variation.
Synthesis-dependent ordering and transitions can cause the quantitative prediction improvement to vary.
The scaling of dual-porosity effects and the simulation of non-equilibrium local ordering create uncertainty in the model's quantitative gain.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome quantifies a 15–20% improvement in prediction accuracy, whereas the falsification rule tests whether selected materials have a 15–20% greater thermal-conductivity reduction. Prediction error and conductivity reduction are different metrics, so the stated benchmark does not directly test the quantified accuracy claim.
